PTA DRUG DEN

By: Graham Coetzer | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We expose a Pretoria drug nest, and ask why a building a condemned two years ago by Tshwane, is still housing the drug lords

Summary:
The Melgisedek building in PTA central, just opposite the Steve Biko hospital, is home to about 1500 homeless people. But the building is in dire straights - a fire destroyed the roof, and the passages are filled with refuse and sewerage pools. It is also a drug hotspot, with Heroin dealers running the show. The building was set to be condemned two years ago by the City of Tshwane, along with other problem/drug hotspot buildings such as Schubart Park which featured in our Brown Street story, but this has not happened for some reason. These are also apparently the same Heroin suppliers as in the Brown str story.

Further information:
The drug dealing and usage on the premises are happening on a large scale, and leading to other criminal activities. Residents of the building are complaining about a NGO called Step Up - they supply clean needles and injections to drug users in exchange for old, used ones in an attempt to curb the spread of related diseases such as HIV - but the area is literally littered with used needles.

I will be joining the PTA Moot CPF on a visit to the buildings and will be filming undercover. Also we have managed to secure a vantage point from a block of flats next to Melgisedek from which we should be able to see a lot of the drug dealing and usage. The CPF might have a heroin user who would be willing to help the investigation. There is a possibility that the same users who helped us get hiddencam footage from Brown Street would be willing to do the same here.

We will be interviewing Step Up on the needle issue as well as City of Tshwane on why demolition of the building has not taken place

Press Release:


Prinshof Drug Den
Amid piles of rubbish, discarded heroin needles and seeping sewage water, children play unsupervised while their destitute parents eke out a living. The Melchizedek building, owned by the Tshwane council, was condemned in 2014 and deemed unfit for human habitation. But, it has become a hotbed of drugs, squalor and rampant crime. How did an abandoned Pretoria building become home to over a thousand heroin addicts, criminals and homeless people?


Script:


PTA Drug Den
Script
29 Feb 2016

Voice
The 11th of February this year, and our cameras accompany a joint Community Policing Forum and SAPS operation near the Pretoria CBD. The CPF want to search several blocks of flats known as Melchizedek for heroin users and dealers. Only a few seconds into the search and the first evidence of drug use on the premises, two unused syringes, are found.

Sound Up Suspect
Man: It’s not mine boss.

CPF: Why is it lying here?

Man: Its people who live here.

Voice
Melchizedek is a cluster of several buildings located on one property just opposite the Steve Biko Academic Hospital. It’s owned by the city of Tshwane, and was condemned in January 2014. But nothing much has come from that resolution. Several hundred homeless people of all races currently inhabit the buildings. Prostitution and drug use are rife. The electricity supply has been cut, there are no working toilets, and mountains of rubbish and raw sewerage litter the halls. We found several young, unsupervised children playing amongst the filth and abandoned needles.

Sound Up Police
Listen, we are placing you under arrest that we have the suspicion that you are in possession of drugs.

Voice
The search did not lead to any major drug finds, but two men were arrested for possession of Heroin.

Sound Up Stephany Potze
This is a notoriously and well-known drug den, where there is both trade in drugs and also use in drugs on the premises.

Voice
Stephany Potze is a member of the Moot Sector 1 Community Policing Forum. She says Melchizedek poses a serious threat to the community of Riviera.




Sound Up Stephany
Stephany: It’s an absolute derelict building. There is absolutely no plumbing or electricity in the building, so inside the building there is great concern of public health issues for the occupants of this building.

Devi: But why is the City not fixing this building, or dealing with the problem here?

Stephany: We have taken this concern to our ward councilors on numerous occasions; our ward councilors have informed us that they have passed it on to the relevant role players, which include national departments as well as the City of Tshwane, but there just appears to be no reaction.

Voice
Blessing Manale is the city’s executive head of public affairs and mayoral spokesperson. He says Tshwane became aware of the problems at Melchizedek in 2013.

Sound Up Blessing Manale
It’s a city owned building on rental stock, it is actually dilapidated beyond human habitation and that’s when we started knowing that we have got to do something about it.

Voice
In 2014 the city condemned the buildings, but Blessing says budget constraints have prevented the city from taking action.

Sound Up Blessing
Once you move people, particularly because you are the landlord, you have got to give them alternative accommodation. And at that time you would remember that we were sitting with two other major cases that had gone to the constitutional court, which was Kruger Park and Schubart Park, where we’d actually been ordered to relocate residents. And that project was costing us in excess of about R50 to R60 million a year.

Voice
So the decision was made to put plans for Melchizedek on hold, which meant that the urban decay continued unabated.

Link Devi
Residents tell us they resent being stereotyped as criminals. There’s a very strong sense of community here and they’re just grateful they have a roof above their heads.

Sound Up Ronnie Williams
They are one of those people who are looking at this place from a spectator’s point of view. That are categorizing people that are staying here. Looking at the building and thinking that the people that are staying here are thinking and are like the building.

Voice
Ronnie Williams is a long time resident of Melchizedek. He says that residents are often blamed for crimes committed by outsiders who use the buildings as a handy hideaway.

Sound Up Ronnie
If someone could rob someone there and he comes running into this place, the people that you see around you, will catch him. That’s what happens here.

Voice
Ronnie moved to Pretoria from Upington when his mother got a job here at Home Affairs. He found employment at a well-known restaurant franchise.

Sound Up Ronnie
Ronnie: As a front-of-house manager. Trainee manager. I was training waiters. We were going around and opening shops and stuff like that.

Devi: Then what happened?

Ronnie: No, I think I started getting exposed to certain things that you know…

Devi: Drugs?

Ronnie: …that just brought me down you know.

Devi: Do you do drugs?

Ronnie: Ja I do drugs.

Devi: And once you’re in you’re in right?

Ronnie: Exactly.

Voice
Ronnie offered to take us on an impromptu tour of the buildings. The first stop: A section residents refer to as the hall of Jerusalem, located at the back of the buildings

Sound Up Ronnie
Devi: Why is it called the hall of Jerusalem?

Ronnie: Because it’s like a source of relief to everyone who doesn’t have a place to stay. It’s like a small heaven for people that are coming from the street.

Voice
To an outsider this particular slice of “heaven” fails to live up to it’s name. At the door we found the usual drug paraphernalia, while the inside was infested with lice and cockroaches, offered very little privacy and suffered from overcrowding.

Sound Up Ronnie
Devi: On one mattress like this how many people would sleep here?

Ronnie: On this one? There is three people sleeping here.

Devi: Three guys? And where has everybody gone now?

Ronnie: They went out to hustle.

Devi: Which means what? Looking for work?

Ronnie: Food, money…

Voice
The conditions here are so poor some people prefer to sleep outside.

Sound Up Ronnie
Devi: So why are there beds outside as well?

Ronnie: Inside there is bugs.

Devi: What bugs?

Ronnie: Those things, “luise”. Lice.

Devi: Lice

Ronnie: So the guys prefer to sleep outside.

Sound Up Devi
So this is the bathroom?

Voice
Walking through the grounds of Melchizedek it’s hard to believe that anyone would want to live there.

Link Devi
Melgisedek is a known drug hotspot. Dealers and users operate in between families and those simply trying to earn an honest living.

Sound Up “Kevin”
Devi: First of all what is that? Is this Nyaope or…?

Kevin: It’s Nyaope, Heroin.

Devi: And how much is that?

Kevin: It’s R25.

Voice
This man, who we’ll call Kevin, is a full-blown heroin addict. He is young and literate, but his addiction has left him both jobless and without a roof over his head. He now calls Melchizedek home.

Sound Up “Kevin”
Kevin: Then I burn it.

Devi: How many times do you do this per day?

Kevin: Eish, I do it a lot of times, maybe five times per day.

Voice
After heating the heroin powder to a brown liquid, Kevin is ready to inject his second hit of the day, a practice junkies call spiking.

Sound Up “Kevin”
Devi: What goes through your mind if you don’t spike?

Kevin: Eish, it’s driving me crazy like… eish. I would do anything for it, to get it, you understand?

Voice
The scars from his repeated heroin abuse are so prominent Kevin uses them to find his veins.

Sound Up “Kevin”
Kevin: You see? You must wait for the blood to come in, to show you, you have the right vein, you see?

Devi: Can you feel it going through your whole body?

Kevin: Yes I can feel it.

Devi: And how do you feel?

Kevin: Now I can say I feel… I feel nice and high you understand?


Voice
Blessing admits the city has not taken the appropriate measures to solve the problems at Melchizedek.

Sound Up Blessing
Devi: It can’t be left like this, it’s just getting worse by the day.
Blessing: Actually by now I think we should have received a condemnation to say we have flouted the laws, but it’s better to keep a person under a tent then to throw them into the street, that we acknowledge ja.

Voice
According to the CPF the drug use at Melchizedek is leading to other crime in the area.

Sound Up Stephany
Most of the crime that you find in the suburb of Riviera is petty theft, where it would be breaking into property and stealing items that can be quickly pawned for their next fix, such as laptops and things.

Voice
And they’re at loggerheads with a local NGO called Step Up that runs a harm reduction project at Melchizedek.

Sound Up Nelson Medeiros
Nelson: Step Up is a harm reduction program. It’s running in the city of Pretoria, Durban and Cape Town simultaneously. In South Africa we have an estimated 67 000 people injecting drugs, and we don’t have a comprehensive set of services for people.

Voice
Nelson Medeiros is a project coordinator for Step Up. He says Step Up’s interventions are endorsed by the World Health Organization and have been proven to reduce rates of HIV infections and other blood-borne diseases such as Hepatitis amongst drug users.

Sound Up Nelson
It’s known as a needle and syringe program, so we give people sterile injecting equipment, which is sterile water, sterile syringes, filters and alcohol swabs… We do wound care, we do HIV counseling and testing… but the core of the project is a HIV prevention project.

Voice
At Melchizedek users have to bring back their used needles and syringes in order to receive clean new ones from Step Up. But the CPF don’t support the program.

Sound Up Stephany
… there is no controlled method of cleaning up this medical hazardous waste. It then just gets strewn over the pavements in our area

Sound Up Nelson
Service delivery starts and our return rate is doing fine, people are bringing syringes back. CPF start programs, start operations, and needles start ending up on the floor. And the reason why syringes are ending up on the floor is because they are being arrested for a syringe… You can’t arrest someone because they are about to break the law.

Voice
Ronnie says he is trying to clean up his life and hopefully start somewhere fresh.

Sound Up Ronnie
Devi: If you had a choice would you stay here?

Ronnie: No

Devi: Where would you want to live?

Ronnie: Like everybody else, in a place that’s got proper living conditions.

Voice
Ultimately it is the City of Tshwane’s responsibility to sort out the problem. Their plan is to partner with a social investor who could fund the relocation of the residents and renovate the buildings in exchange for favorable subsidies from the City.

Sound Up Blessing
Devi: Is it going to take another four years before something is done?

Blessing: We would put our heads on the block if we don’t see something much more better by the end of this year, towards the end of this year. We don’t want a similar Christmas for those people than they have seen for the last three or four Christmases.
